title: Long Ago and Today
bigQuestion: How do we know what life was like long ago?

story.title: Grandma's Shoebox
story.kicker: A box under the bed holds a phone with a dial, an old ticket and a photo of a girl.
paragraphs: Maya is at Grandma's house in Chicago. She finds a shoebox under the bed. The box is dusty. Grandma smiles. "Open it," she says. "Those are my things from long ago."
Inside is a heavy black phone. It has a round dial with holes. No screen. No buttons. "You put your finger in a hole and turn it," Grandma says. "One number at a time. It took a while."

Under the phone is a paper ticket. It is small and yellow. It says "Chicago, Illinois." Grandma rode a train with it when she was six. Under the ticket is a photo. A girl stands in front of a school. She has braids.
"Who is that?" Maya asks. "That is me," says Grandma. "That was my school." Maya looks at the girl in the photo. Then she looks at Grandma. Same smile. Long ago, Grandma was a kid too.
story.think: What is one old thing in your home? What can it tell you about long ago?

lessons.title: Yesterday, Today, Tomorrow
lessons.mainIdea: The past is before now, the present is now, and the future is after now.
reading: Think about yesterday. What did you eat? What did you play? Yesterday is over. It is in the *past*. The past is all the time before now.
Now think about right now. You are reading. You are sitting. This is the *present*. The present is now, this very minute.
Tomorrow has not come yet. It is in the *future*. The future is the time after now. Long ago is the past. Someday is the future. Today is the present.

words.d: the time before now, like yesterday or long ago
the time after now, like tomorrow or next year

look.title: Three Pictures of a Tree
look.text: Look at the first picture. A small girl plants a tiny tree. Look at the second picture. The girl is bigger. The tree is as tall as she is. Look at the third picture. The tree is huge. A grown woman sits under it with her own kids.
look.prompt: Which picture is the past? Which is the present? Which is the future?

check.q: Yesterday is in the what?
check.why: Yesterday is over. It is before now. That is the past.

check.q: What is the present?
check.why: The present is now, this very minute.

check.q: Tomorrow is in the what?
check.why: Tomorrow has not come yet. The time after now is the future.

lessons.title: Old Things Are Clues
lessons.mainIdea: Old photos and objects are clues that tell us about the past.
reading: We were not alive long ago. So how do we know about it? We look for *clues*. A clue is a thing that helps you figure something out. Old things are clues.
An old photo is a clue. Look at the clothes. Look at the cars. Look at the street. Each one tells you something. A photo is a piece of the past you can hold.
Grandma's dial phone is a clue too. It shows how people called each other. Old things like this are called *artifacts*. An artifact is an object made by people long ago.

words.d: a thing that helps you figure something out
an object made or used by people long ago

look.title: The Old Photo
look.text: Look at the photo. It is black and white, not color. A boy stands by a street. He wears short pants and a cap. Behind him is a car with big round lights and thin tires. A horse pulls a wagon down the same street.
look.prompt: Name three clues in the photo that show it was taken long ago.

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: A new toy from the store
check.why: An artifact is an object made or used by people long ago.

check.q: How do we learn about the past?
choices: We wait for it to come
check.why: Old photos and old things are clues. They tell us about the past.

check.q: A photo shows a horse pulling a wagon on a street. What is that a clue for?
choices: The photo is from long ago
The photo is from the future
check.why: Long ago, horses pulled wagons on streets. That is a clue about the past.

lessons.title: Getting From Here to There
lessons.mainIdea: How people travel has changed a lot over time.
reading: Long ago, there were no cars. People walked. Or they rode a horse. Or a horse pulled their wagon. A trip to the next town took all day.
Then came trains. A train ran on rails. It carried many people fast. In Chicago, trains ran on tracks up in the air. People called it the "L." It is still there today.
Then came cars, buses and planes. Today a car ride to the next town takes minutes. A plane can cross the country in one day. *Travel* got faster and faster.

words.d: to go from one place to another place

look.title: The Same Trip
look.text: Look at the road to Grandma's town. Long ago, a boy rode there in a wagon. The horse walked all day. The boy got there at night. Today, a girl rides there in a car. She leaves after lunch. She gets there before dinner.
look.prompt: What changed? What stayed the same about the trip?

check.q: How did people travel long ago, before cars?
check.why: Long ago there were no cars. People walked or used horses and wagons.

check.q: What is the "L" in Chicago?
choices: A train on tracks up in the air
check.why: The "L" is a train that runs on tracks up in the air. It is still used today.

check.q: How did travel change over time?
check.why: Wagons were slow. Trains, cars and planes are much faster.

lessons.title: Cooking and Talking
lessons.mainIdea: Cooking and talking to far-away people changed as new tools were made.
reading: Long ago, people cooked on a wood *stove*. First you had to chop wood. Then you lit a fire. Then you waited for the stove to get hot. Cooking took a long time.
Today many people cook on a gas or electric stove. You turn a knob. It gets hot right away. Some people use a microwave. Dinner can be ready in minutes.
Talking changed too. Long ago, people wrote letters. A letter took days to arrive. Then came the phone with a dial. Today we use cell phones. We can talk or text right away.

words.d: a thing you cook food on

look.title: Two Kitchens
look.text: Look at the first kitchen. A big iron stove sits by the wall. A pile of wood sits next to it. A girl carries water in a bucket. Look at the second kitchen. A white stove has knobs. A microwave sits on the counter. Water comes from a sink.
look.prompt: Which kitchen is from long ago? How can you tell?

check.q: What did people burn in a stove long ago?
check.why: Long ago, people chopped wood and burned it in the stove.

check.q: How did people talk to far-away friends long ago?
choices: They called on a cell phone
check.why: Long ago there were no phones. People wrote letters that took days to arrive.

check.q: Why is cooking faster today?
check.why: Gas and electric stoves get hot right away. No wood to chop, no fire to build.

lessons.title: School Long Ago
lessons.mainIdea: Schools long ago had one room, one teacher and no computers.
reading: Long ago, many towns had a *one-room school*. All the kids sat in one room. Little kids and big kids. One teacher taught them all.
Kids wrote on small boards called slates. They used chalk. Then they wiped it off. There were no computers. There was no bus. Kids walked to school, even in snow.
Some things are the same. Kids learned to read. Kids did math. Kids played at recess. Ask a grown-up what their school was like. What did they have? What did they not have?

words.d: a school long ago where all the kids learned in one room

look.title: Ask Grandpa
look.text: Maya asks Grandpa about his school. He says, "We had a chalkboard, not a screen. We had a big bell that rang. We had no computers. But we had recess. And we had a mean kickball game."
look.prompt: What is one thing that changed? What is one thing that stayed the same?

check.q: What did kids write on long ago?
check.why: Kids wrote on small boards called slates. They used chalk and wiped it off.

check.q: In a one-room school, who taught the little kids and the big kids?
check.why: All the kids sat in one room. One teacher taught them all.

check.q: What is one thing that stayed the same at school?
check.why: Kids learned to read long ago too. Buses and computers are new.

lessons.title: A Town in One Hundred Years
lessons.mainIdea: A town can change a lot in one hundred years, and old maps and photos show how.
reading: Picture a small town one hundred years ago. It has a dirt road. It has a store, a church and a school. Farms are all around it. Horses stand by the store.
Now picture the same town today. The road is paved. There are more houses. There is a gas station. There is a big store. Cars are parked where the horses stood.
How do we know the town *changed*? We look at old maps. We look at old photos. We count the people. Chicago was a small town once. Now it is a big city.

look.title: How Many People Lived in Chicago
look.prompt: When did Chicago have the fewest people? When did it have the most?

check.q: What was the road like in the town one hundred years ago?
check.why: The old town had a dirt road. Today the road is paved.

check.q: How can we tell a town changed?
choices: We look at old maps and photos
check.why: Old maps and photos are clues. They show how a place looked before.

check.q: Chicago in 1850 had about how many people?
check.why: The chart shows about thirty thousand people in 1850. It was a small town.

lessons.title: Families, Play and Food
lessons.mainIdea: Some things stay the same over time, like families, play and eating together.
reading: Not everything changes. Long ago, kids lived with families. Families cared for each other. That is still true today. Families are a thing that stayed the *same*.
Kids played long ago too. They played tag. They jumped rope. They played with dolls and balls. Toys look different now. But kids still love to play.
Families ate together long ago. They ate bread, soup and corn. Today we still eat bread and soup and corn. The food came from a farm then. It comes from a farm now.

look.title: Jump Rope, Then and Now
look.text: Look at the old photo. Three girls jump rope on a sidewalk. They wear long dresses. Look at the new photo. Three girls jump rope on a sidewalk. They wear shorts and sneakers. Both groups are laughing.
look.prompt: What changed in the two photos? What stayed the same?

check.q: Which thing stayed the same over time?
check.why: Long ago and today, families care for each other. Phones and wagons changed.

check.q: Did kids play long ago?
choices: Yes, they played tag and jumped rope
check.why: Kids long ago played tag, jumped rope and played with balls.

check.q: Where did food come from long ago and today?
check.why: Food came from a farm then. It still comes from a farm now.

lessons.title: A Timeline of My Life
lessons.mainIdea: A timeline puts events in order from first to last.
reading: A *timeline* is a line with events on it. The first thing goes on the left. The last thing goes on the right. It shows what came first and what came next.
Make a timeline of your life. First: you were born. Next: you learned to walk. Next: you lost a tooth. Next: you started school. Draw each one on the line.
A family timeline is longer. Ask a grown-up. When were they born? When did they start school? Put their events on the line. Put yours after. Now you see the past and the present together.

words.d: a line that shows events in order, first to last

look.title: Maya's Timeline
look.text: Look at Maya's timeline. On the left it says "Born." Next it says "First steps." Next it says "Baby brother." Next it says "Lost a tooth." On the right it says "Started first grade."
look.prompt: Which event came first? Which came last? What might Maya add next?

check.q: On a timeline, where does the first event go?
check.why: The first thing goes on the left. The last thing goes on the right.

check.q: Which event would come first on your timeline?
check.why: You were born before you did anything else. It goes first.

check.q: Why ask a grown-up for a family timeline?
choices: They know events from before you were born
check.why: Grown-ups lived in the past before you. They can tell you what happened.

review.q: Long ago is in the what?
review.why: Long ago is before now. That is the past.
An old photo shows clothes, cars and streets from long ago. It is a clue.

review.q: Before cars, how did people travel far?
review.why: Long ago, people walked or rode horses. A horse pulled the wagon.

review.q: What did kids use to write on in a one-room school?
review.why: Kids wrote on slates with chalk. There were no computers.

review.q: Which one stayed the same from long ago to today?
choices: The kind of phone we use
review.why: Kids played long ago and play today. Phones and stoves changed.

review.q: On a timeline, the last event goes where?
review.why: First goes on the left. Last goes on the right.
